title: D.C. CRIMES Act
official_title: To limit youth offender status in the District of Columbia to individuals 18 years of age or younger, to direct the Attorney General of the District of Columbia to establish and operate a publicly accessible website containing updated statistics on juvenile crime in the District of Columbia, to amend the District of Columbia Home Rule Act to prohibit the Council of the District of Columbia from enacting changes to existing criminal liability sentences, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Received in the Senate on September 17, 2025 after House action; no further Senate action recorded. Sponsored by a Republican member with eight cosponsors and referred in the House to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
summary: Amends the District of Columbia Youth Rehabilitation Act of 1985 to lower the age ceiling for "youth offender" status from "24 years of age or younger" to "18 years of age or younger" (Section 2(6) of the Youth Rehabilitation Act, D.C. Official Code section 24-901(6)). Two conforming amendments follow: Section 3(a-1) of the Act (D.C. Official Code section 24-902(a-1)) is amended by striking paragraph (3) (which addressed strategic planning for individuals 18 through 24 in facilities, treatment, and services), and Section 4(a)(2) (D.C. Official Code section 24-903(a)(2)) is amended to change "15 to 24 years of age" to "15 to 18 years of age." Section 4(b) (D.C. Official Code section 24-903(b)) is restructured — paragraph (2) (which addressed sentencing below the mandatory-minimum term) is struck and paragraph (3) is redesignated as paragraph (2). Section 3 adds a new section 16-2340a to Subchapter I of chapter 23 of title 16, D.C. Official Code, requiring the D.C. Attorney General to establish and operate a publicly accessible website with 11 juvenile-crime data measures (arrests by year, arrests broken down by age/race/sex, petty crime arrests, crime-of-violence arrests, first-offense arrests, prior-arrest history, declination rates, adult-court transfers, sentencing outcomes, and time-served information), updated monthly and archived, in a machine-readable bulk-download format, and without personally identifiable information. Conforming amendments (D.C. Code sections 16-2331, 16-2332, and 16-2333) allow the release of juvenile case, social, and law-enforcement records to the D.C. Attorney General for the website. The website must be established within 180 days of enactment. Section 4 amends section 602(a) of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act (D.C. Code section 1-206.02(a)) to prohibit the D.C. Council from enacting any act, resolution, or rule to change any criminal liability sentence in effect on the date of enactment of the D.C. CRIMES Act.
brief: Lowers the D.C. "youth offender" ceiling from 24 to 18, restricts sub-mandatory-minimum sentencing for that group, requires the D.C. Attorney General to run a monthly-updated public juvenile-crime statistics website with 11 specified data measures, and bars the D.C. Council from changing existing criminal liability sentences.

top_lines.headline: Juvenile Crime Statistics Website (Section 16-2340a)
subs: D.C. Attorney General must establish and operate a publicly accessible website

11 required statistical measures: total arrests annually; arrests by age/race/sex; petty-crime arrests (vandalism, theft, shoplifting); crime-of-violence arrests; first-offense arrests; prior-arrest history; number of prior arrests among repeat arrestees; declination rate for OAG prosecutions; number tried as adults; sentencing outcomes (no sentence / misdemeanor / felony); length of correctional-facility time to be served
Updated monthly; archived for indefinite historical access; available in machine-readable bulk-download format; no personally identifiable information
Website must be established within 180 days of enactment

top_lines.headline: Bar on D.C. Council Sentence Changes
subs: Section 602(a) of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act (D.C. Code section 1-206.02(a)) amended by adding paragraph (11)
Prohibits the D.C. Council from enacting any act, resolution, or rule to change any criminal liability sentence in effect on the date of enactment of the D.C. CRIMES Act

items.main: Names the Act the "DC Criminal Reforms to Immediately Make Everyone Safe Act" or the "DC CRIMES Act."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Amends Section 2(6) of the Youth Rehabilitation Act of 1985 (D.C. Code section 24-901(6)) by striking "24 years of age or younger" and inserting "18 years of age or younger."
items.detail: This is the operative age-ceiling change. Two conforming amendments follow: Section 3(a-1) paragraph (3) (D.C. Code section 24-902(a-1)) is struck (it addressed strategic planning for individuals 18 through 24 in facilities, treatment, and services), and Section 4(a)(2) (D.C. Code section 24-903(a)(2)) is amended by striking "15 to 24 years of age" and inserting "15 to 18 years of age."

items.main: Amends Section 4(b) of the Act (D.C. Code section 24-903(b)) to strike the "(b)(1)" designation and insert "(b)," strike paragraph (2), and redesignate paragraph (3) as paragraph (2). This removes the paragraph that addressed sentencing below the mandatory-minimum term.
items.detail: Restructures the subsection so that only the redesignated paragraph (2) (formerly (3)) remains after the base subsection (b).

sections.label: Section 3 — Establishment and Operation of Website on District of Columbia Juvenile Crime Statistics

items.main: Adds new section 16-2340a to Subchapter I of chapter 23 of title 16, D.C. Official Code, requiring the D.C. Attorney General to establish and operate a publicly accessible website containing 11 juvenile-crime statistical measures.
items.detail: The 11 measures are: (1) total juveniles arrested each year; (2) totals and percentages by age, race, and sex; (3) petty-crime arrests (vandalism, theft, shoplifting); (4) crime-of-violence arrests (as defined in D.C. Code section 23-1331(4)); (5) first-offense arrests; (6) prior-arrest history; (7) number of prior arrests among the previously-arrested cohort; (8) declination rate for prosecutions by the D.C. Office of the Attorney General; (9) number tried as adults; (10) sentencing outcomes (no sentence / misdemeanor / felony); (11) length of correctional-facility time to be served.

items.main: Requires monthly updates, indefinite archival, and machine-readable bulk-download format; prohibits inclusion of personally identifiable information. Defines "crime" (per D.C. Code section 23-1331(2) "offense") and "juvenile" (per Section 2(6) of the Youth Rehabilitation Act, as amended by this bill).

Conforming records-access amendments: D.C. Code section 16-2331 (juvenile case records) new subsection (i); section 16-2332 (juvenile social records) new subsection (h); section 16-2333 (police and other law enforcement records) new subsection (g) — each requiring a person to provide the specified records to the Attorney General for purposes of the website established under section 16-2340a.
items.detail: Each amendment overrides the applicable confidentiality provision of the underlying section (subsections (b) or (a) as noted in the text).

items.main: Effective date: the D.C. Attorney General must establish the website within 180 days of enactment.
items.detail: Subsection (c) of Section 3. Note the effective-date subsection references "section 16-2341" though subsection (a) adds section 16-2340a — the deadline applies to the website established under the new section.

sections.label: Section 4 — Prohibiting Council From Enacting Changes to Existing Criminal Liability Sentences

items.main: Amends Section 602(a) of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act (D.C. Code section 1-206.02(a)) by adding a new paragraph (11) that prohibits the D.C. Council from enacting any act, resolution, or rule to change any criminal liability sentence in effect on the date of enactment of the D.C. CRIMES Act.
items.detail: Section 602(a) of the Home Rule Act lists limitations on the Council's legislative authority; paragraph (11) is added at the end. Conforming edits change "or" at the end of paragraph (9) to a semicolon, and the period at the end of paragraph (10) to "; or."

gaps: The bill does not modify or replace the confidentiality standards that would otherwise apply to juvenile case, social, and law-enforcement records — the amendments override those standards only for the website reporting purpose.
The bill does not describe how the D.C. Attorney General is to handle transitional cases involving individuals aged 19 through 24 who currently receive youth offender treatment.
The bill does not authorize funding for the D.C. Attorney General to establish or operate the website.
The bill does not create an enforcement mechanism or judicial-review pathway for the paragraph (11) Council prohibition.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Donalds
featured_quotes.text: Now, in reference to what the gentleman was just talking about, Article I, Section 8, Clause 17 of the United States Constitution is quite clear. It grants Congress the power to exercise exclusive, exclusive jurisdiction over the Federal District, which all Americans know now is Washington, D.C., and it is the Nation's Capital. That is in the Constitution that was ratified by several States. Congress does have the constitutional authority to regulate activities within the Federal District.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Boebert
featured_quotes.text: This critical legislation is a direct response to the failed pro-crime policies that have turned our Nation's Capital into a war zone. Under failing leftist policies, Washington, D.C., has seen an epidemic of violence: carjackings surging 300 percent, homicides ravaging communities, and young thugs, some as old as 24, treated as juveniles, slapped with lenient sentences below mandatory minimums. It endangers young families and small businesses struggling in this crime-ridden city.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hageman
featured_quotes.text: There is no question that there has been a crime epidemic across the District of Columbia, and the citizens of this great city deserve better. President Trump recognized this fact and has exercised his authority to restore safety. It is now time for Congress to build on his good work. H.R. 4922 is designed to begin to address many of the problems that stem from the D.C. courts and their refusal to hold criminals accountable. We need to start with recognizing that 19- to 24-year-olds shouldn't be treated as youthful offenders.
